title: The Lost Bronze Computer
facts: The Antikythera mechanism was retrieved from a Roman cargo ship wreck off the Greek island Antikythera in 1901, probably in July.
Greek politician Spyridon Stais noticed a gear in the artifact in 1902 during a museum visit, prompting study by his cousin Valerios Stais.
The device is housed in a wooden‑framed case measuring about 34 cm × 18 cm × 9 cm (13.4 in × 7.1 in × 3.5 in).
The largest gear is roughly 13 cm (5 in) in diameter and originally had 223 teeth.
Imaging in 2005 revealed the mechanism contained 35 meshing bronze gears, 30 of which are still visible.
It could predict astronomical positions, eclipses, and track the four‑year cycle of the ancient Olympic Games.
All fragments are kept at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, displayed with reconstructions and replicas.
The shipwreck that carried the mechanism dates to approximately 70–60 BC, so the device must be older than that.
Its construction is dated variously to about 87 BC, between 150 and 100 BC, or 205 BC, making it centuries older than any known medieval analogue computer.
Machines of comparable complexity did not reappear until the 14th century in western Europe.

lines.say: In 1901, a diver pulls a bronze box.
He lifts the wooden case measuring 34 cm × 18 cm × 9 cm.
Spyridon Stais spots a gear and calls his cousin.
Valerios Stais opens the device and sees bronze teeth.
Imaging in 2005 shows thirty visible gears interlocking.
Archaeologists think it predicts eclipses and Olympic cycles.
The largest gear holds two hundred twenty‑three teeth.
Its age predates Gutenberg's press by centuries.
All fragments rest in the National Archaeological Museum.
The device sits in a wooden‑framed case for viewers.
And nobody knows why it vanished from history.
Could this ancient computer outsmart modern machines?
